Each item records its specific risk_reason and audit_focus.

The Four-Case item relies on appropriate full secondary passages because Pereboom’s 2001 Chapter 4 text was not accessible; that limitation is explicit, and an unverified public excerpt is not counted as evidence. The brain-bisection article now specifies that the Pinto comparison result was from Patient DDC only. None is expert_reviewed.

entries.title: Split Brains and the Unity of Consciousness
entries.scope: Claim-level traceability review of the complete article, matching dataset record, and expansion entry. Focus: classic split-brain methods and task-specific findings; limits of inference from everyday behavior; Nagel’s argument about unity and subject-count; current interpretive models; and Pinto et al.’s 2017 detection/localization and cross-hemifield comparison results. This status records source traceability, not settled neuroscience, the truth of a theory of consciousness, expert review, or exhaustive literature coverage.
entries.summary: The classic primary reports support task- and response-dependent dissociations, with patient and testing limits preserved. Nagel’s full 1971 paper supports the philosophical question and his indeterminate-count conclusion, which the article distinguishes from an empirical result. Current SEP and the 2020 review represent the unity debate as open. Pinto et al. support the precise distinction now stated: both patients detected and localized stimuli across the field, while the separate cross-hemifield comparison was tested on Patient DDC alone and was not significantly above chance. The final independent reviewer confirmed that scope; the article and evidence record now specify the exact Pinto sections consulted. No expert review is claimed.

sources.exact_locations_read: Printed pp. 1765–1769, including the patient and surgical history, visual and visuomotor test results, and discussion of response-dependent performance and case limitations.
sources.limitations: A small historical clinical case series cannot establish a single consciousness model or generalize identically to every patient. The report notes the case’s history and pre-existing brain injury; it is used for the specific test dissociations it reports.

sources.title: Split-Brain: What We Know Now and Why This is Important for Understanding Consciousness
sources.author: Edward H. F. de Haan, Paul M. Corballis, Steven A. Hillyard, Carlo A. Marzi, Anil Seth, Victor A. F. Lamme, Lukas Volz, Mara Fabri, Elizabeth Schechter, Tim Bayne, Michael Corballis, and Yair Pinto

sources.title: Split brain: divided perception but undivided consciousness
sources.author: Yair Pinto, David A. Neville, Marte Otten, Paul M. Corballis, Victor A. F. Lamme, Edward H. F. de Haan, Nicoletta Foschi, and Mara Fabri
sources.access_level: Relevant full-text HTML sections were accessed and read; the subscription-only PDF was not required for the cited claims.
sources.exact_locations_read: Patients and methods—Subjects/Procedure; Results, Experiments 1–2; Discussion. Experiment 1 reports detection and localization across the visual field for both DDC and DDV across response types. Experiment 2 reports cross-hemifield comparisons for Patient DDC only; mean performance was 55.4%, not significantly above chance (all stimulus categories P > 0.25).
sources.limitations: Only two patients were studied; the cross-hemifield comparison result was from DDC, not both patients. The authors’ unified-consciousness interpretation is a contested interpretation, not a settled refutation of earlier dissociation findings.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Classic split-brain tests can reveal response- and task-dependent dissociations after commissurotomy, including differences between verbal naming and hand selection for lateralized stimuli.
claim_evidence.source_title: Some Functional Effects of Sectioning the Cerebral Commissures in Man
claim_evidence.exact_location: Printed pp. 1765–1769, especially visual and visuomotor test results and discussion; corroborated by Sperry (1968), pp. 723–727, on lateralized testing and separate verbal/hand responses.
claim_evidence.finding: The primary reports support the article’s description of controlled tests and response-dependent dissociations. The revised article specifies that results vary with patient, extent of disconnection, task, and response.
claim_evidence.limitation: These tests do not establish that every patient has two subjects or that every everyday function is divided. The 1962 report concerns specific patients and procedures.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: qualified the empirical summary by patient, surgery, task, and response; avoided inferring separate persons from the classic tests.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Ordinary social behavior cannot by itself settle whether split-brain experience is unified or divided.
claim_evidence.source_title: Split-Brain: What We Know Now and Why This is Important for Understanding Consciousness
claim_evidence.exact_location: Review abstract and Conclusions on insufficient evidence; SEP §§3.1 and 3.1.1 on the evidential limits of everyday behavior; Nagel, pp. 401–402 and 406–409, for the contrast between ordinary life and experimental dissociation.
claim_evidence.finding: The article does not describe everyday behavior as fully normal or as resolving the unity question; it presents ordinary integration and controlled dissociation as evidence that require interpretation.
claim_evidence.limitation: The review reports that some functional integration may remain and that the mechanisms and subjective implications remain disputed.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: removed a categorical implication that everyday behavior proves normal integration or a single subject.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Nagel argues that the ordinary concepts of mind and person do not yield a determinate one-or-two answer for split-brain cases.
claim_evidence.source_title: Brain Bisection and the Unity of Consciousness
claim_evidence.exact_location: Printed pp. 406–409, especially the concluding discussion of experimental evidence, ordinary integration, and the difficulty of assigning a whole-number count of minds; SEP discussion of Nagel in §3.1 provides context.
claim_evidence.finding: The article attributes this as Nagel’s philosophical conclusion, distinct from the underlying clinical results and from a settled neuroscience claim.
claim_evidence.limitation: This establishes what Nagel argued, not that his conceptual conclusion is uniquely correct.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: separated Nagel’s argument from empirical findings and framed it as his view.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Current accounts include two-stream, single-stream, partial-stream, and hybrid models, and the model chosen does not by itself settle identity over time.
claim_evidence.exact_location: SEP §§3.1, 3.1.1, and 3.1.3, on split-brain theories, differences between experimental and everyday contexts, and the structure of consciousness.
claim_evidence.finding: The article presents the taxonomy as competing proposals and does not identify a single model as consensus.
claim_evidence.limitation: The classification is a concise summary; individual theories and hybrids have additional distinctions.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: listed proposals as competing models and stated that they do not independently settle personal identity.

claim_evidence.material_claim: In Pinto et al.’s 2017 study, both patients detected and localized stimuli across the visual field, while the cross-hemifield comparison result was tested on Patient DDC alone and was not significantly above chance.
claim_evidence.source_title: Split brain: divided perception but undivided consciousness
claim_evidence.exact_location: Patients and methods—Subjects/Procedure; Results, Experiment 1 (both patients’ detection/localization); Results, Experiment 2 (cross-hemifield comparison in DDC only, mean 55.4%, not significantly above chance); Discussion.
claim_evidence.finding: The article now distinguishes the two-patient detection/localization result from DDC’s separate comparison task. The paper’s claim that its broader results support undivided consciousness is identified as the authors’ contested interpretation.
claim_evidence.limitation: Two patients cannot establish universal outcomes; the comparison result applies to DDC only and does not erase earlier task-specific dissociations.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: specified Patient DDC for the comparison task, stated that performance was not significantly above chance, and added exact consulted sections to the source-attribution note.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Philosophical extensions and thought prompts about reconnecting a divided brain or identity over time are not presented as clinical evidence.
claim_evidence.exact_location: SEP §§3.1 and 3.1.3, which distinguish theories of unity and implications for the subject from experimental findings.
claim_evidence.finding: The article labels hypothetical reconnection as a philosophical extension and separates identity questions from direct clinical findings.
claim_evidence.limitation: The extension is an editorial teaching prompt rather than a claim established by the cited experiments.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: labelled the reconnection scenario as a philosophical extension, not clinical evidence.

edits_made: Qualified classic empirical findings by patient, disconnection, task, and response; identified the 1962 primary study and cited Sperry’s 1968 synthesis.
Distinguished Nagel’s 1971 philosophical conclusion from empirical neuroscience and from claims about personal identity over time.
Presented current consciousness models as competing interpretations and described the broader evidence as unresolved.
Corrected the Pinto result to distinguish both patients’ detection/localization from the cross-hemifield comparison tested on Patient DDC only.
Recorded the exact Pinto Methods, Results, and Discussion sections consulted in the article and this ledger; aligned dataset references and review date.

The article is a concise educational account, not an exhaustive review of the split-brain literature or every clinical variation.

entries.title: Pereboom’s Four-Case Argument
entries.scope: Claim-level traceability review of the complete article, matching dataset record, and expansion entry. Focus: the four-case progression and like-cases inference; the specified cases and compatibilist-friendly capacities; under-description and disagreement; hard- and soft-line replies; the target of basic-desert responsibility; related manipulation arguments; publication metadata; and accurate disclosure of primary-text access. This status follows the approved standard’s allowance for another appropriate source when relevant passages are read; it does not claim direct verification against Pereboom’s 2001 Chapter 4 or expert review.
entries.summary: Full relevant passages in the archived SEP supplement, current SEP entry, Jeppsson’s peer-reviewed analysis, and Caruso’s précis support the article’s narrowed paraphrase of the cases, conditional inference, known disagreement, and basic-desert scope. The article no longer implies that the primary 2001 chapter was read: Google Books lists Chapter 4 but exposes selected image-only pages rather than its argument text; an online excerpt’s provenance remains unverified and is not treated as verified book text. A targeted independent post-edit reviewer passed the revised access disclosure. An earlier reviewer preferred a partial status because the primary chapter was inaccessible; this ledger adopts source_checked for the declared paraphrase/traceability scope because the appropriate full secondary passages were read and the access limit is explicit. No expert review is claimed.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Pereboom’s four cases move from direct moment-to-moment manipulation, to birth programming, to upbringing, and then to an ordinary agent in a deterministic world; the inference appeals to treating relevantly like cases alike.
claim_evidence.exact_location: Introduction, “The argument,” including the sequence from electronic intervention to programming/upbringing and Case 4; corroborated by Jeppsson §1, pp. 1935–1937.
claim_evidence.finding: The article describes the sequence and makes the inference conditional: a responsibility-relevant difference that blocks the transition to Case 4 would undermine the argument.
claim_evidence.limitation: The cases’ comparability and the like-cases principle are contested; no claim is made that the argument is proven sound.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: presented the transition as an argument with a conditional premise, not as an established equivalence.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Case 1 uses radio-like technology to manipulate Plum’s decisions and actions moment by moment while stipulating compatibilist-friendly capacities, including reasons-responsive deliberation.

claim_evidence.limitation: The article is a stylized thought experiment and compresses case details; no verbatim quotation from the inaccessible 2001 chapter is presented.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The move from the first three cases to ordinary determinism is disputed because the first three cases are under-described and different completions may change whether a responsibility-relevant difference exists.

claim_evidence.finding: The article accurately reports that case details and reader verdicts are contested and does not state that the transition is universally accepted.
claim_evidence.limitation: The brief article does not catalog every response or each proposed detail that could matter.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: added the current SEP qualification that the first three cases are under-described and verdicts can vary with specification.

entries.title: Goodman’s New Riddle of Induction (Grue)
entries.scope: Claim-level traceability review of the complete article, matching dataset record, and expansion entry. Focus: Goodman’s definition of grue and its time cutoff; the conflicting future projections; the distinction between instance-confirmation and the projectibility problem; entrenchment; cited naturalness and Bayesian approaches; and the article’s own teaching analogies. This status records source traceability, not that Goodman’s argument succeeds or that one solution is accepted by consensus.
entries.summary: Goodman’s full-text scan supports the grue definition, incompatible post-cutoff predictions, and the entrenchment discussion. The SEP Goodman and Problem of Induction entries contextualize the new riddle and positionality reply. Fitelson’s paper supports a qualified statement that Bayesian analyses depend on measures and assumptions, while the article explicitly marks its priors/model-class takeaway as an editorial inference. Scholz’s 2024 open-access paper supports identifying conceptual spaces as a particular similarity/naturalness proposal and attributing the normative critique to Scholz, not to consensus. The independent final review found no material issue in the declared scope.

sources.title: Conceptual Spaces: A Solution to Goodman’s New Riddle of Induction?
sources.author: Sebastian Scholz
sources.access_level: Full open-access article was accessed; abstract, introduction, and conclusion were read.
sources.exact_locations_read: Abstract and §1 on Gärdenfors’s conceptual-spaces/similarity proposal; §5 conclusion, pp. 932–934, on the proposal’s current limits as a normative justification.
sources.limitations: Scholz critiques one specific proposal and its current cognitive form; this is not treated as a survey verdict or consensus about every naturalness-based answer.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Goodman defines grue using a fixed future cutoff: an object examined before t is grue if green, while an object not examined before t is grue if blue; the observed emeralds therefore fit both green and grue descriptions before t.
claim_evidence.exact_location: Chapter III §4, pp. 73–75, definition of grue and the emerald illustration; SEP Goodman §5.3 corroborates the new-riddle presentation.
claim_evidence.finding: The article now defines the cutoff explicitly and distinguishes examined-before-t from not-examined-before-t cases.
claim_evidence.limitation: This is a simplified teaching formulation; the book’s fuller formulation is tied to a specified time and examination condition.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: stated the cutoff and examination condition explicitly.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Simple instance-confirmation can leave green and grue with the same observed support while implying incompatible predictions after t; this is Goodman’s projectibility problem, not merely the older Humean question of justifying induction in general.
claim_evidence.exact_location: Chapter III §4, pp. 73–81; SEP Goodman §§5.1–5.3 and SEP Problem of Induction §4.2 for the distinction between the new riddle and induction’s broader justification problem.
claim_evidence.finding: The article explains the prediction conflict under a simple confirmation setup and identifies projectibility as the further problem.
claim_evidence.limitation: The confirmation setup is an explanatory simplification, not a claim that every theory of confirmation assigns identical support in all formulations.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: clarified the simple-confirmation assumption and separated Goodman’s riddle from the broader problem of induction.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Goodman uses entrenchment—how successfully predicates have been projected in past practice—to explain why familiar predicates such as green are favored over grue, while leaving open whether this gives an ultimate normative justification.
claim_evidence.exact_location: Chapter IV §3, printed p. 94; SEP Goodman §5.4 on entrenchment and the distinction between describing actual projection practice and ultimate justification.
claim_evidence.finding: The article attributes entrenchment to Goodman and describes its explanatory role without claiming it ends the normative debate.
claim_evidence.limitation: Entrenchment’s adequacy as a justification remains a philosophical question; the article does not claim otherwise.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: narrowed the description of entrenchment and its explanatory scope.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Conceptual spaces and similarity provide one contemporary naturalness-based approach; Scholz argues that the proposal in its current cognitive form does not supply the needed normative justification.
claim_evidence.source_title: Conceptual Spaces: A Solution to Goodman’s New Riddle of Induction?
claim_evidence.exact_location: Abstract, §1, and §5 conclusion, pp. 932–934; SEP Goodman §5.3 provides background on competing responses.
claim_evidence.finding: The article identifies a specific proposal and attributes its critique to Scholz rather than presenting it as a settled literature-wide verdict.
claim_evidence.limitation: The claim concerns Scholz’s assessment of a particular version of Gärdenfors’s account; it does not rule out all naturalness or similarity theories.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: narrowed the naturalness discussion to the proposal Scholz reviews and stated the critique as his conclusion.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The positionality objection notes that grue/bleen appear dependent on green/blue in a language where green/blue are basic; Goodman’s symmetry response reverses that dependence in a grue/bleen-basic language.
claim_evidence.exact_location: SEP §5.3, discussion of positionality and Goodman’s symmetry response.
claim_evidence.finding: The article presents positionality as an objection and Goodman’s response, then identifies language-invariant naturalness as the remaining issue rather than declaring a winner.
claim_evidence.limitation: The short entry does not exhaust every response to Goodman’s symmetry argument.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: attributed the positionality objection and Goodman’s reply, and limited the article’s conclusion to that exchange.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Bayesian accounts can assign different comparative confirmation results depending on confirmation measures, prior/model classes, bridge assumptions, and background evidence; the article’s model-class takeaway is an editorial inference rather than a direct result attributed to Fitelson.
claim_evidence.exact_location: Fitelson §§3–4 and §6; manuscript pp. 15–16 on measure sensitivity and later discussion/conclusion pp. 21ff on assumptions and total evidence.
claim_evidence.finding: Fitelson’s analysis supports the qualified sensitivity claim. The article labels its broader priors/model-class moral as its own editorial inference.
claim_evidence.limitation: The article is not presented as a survey of every Bayesian analysis; the manuscript text, rather than the publisher-hosted version, was consulted.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: retained the qualification and marked the model-class takeaway as editorial inference.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The machine-learning comparison and place-dependent predicates are teaching analogies/extensions, not historical claims about Goodman’s own examples or a sourced resolution of the riddle.
claim_evidence.exact_location: The article’s explicit framing in §§5 and 7 was compared with Goodman, Chapter III §4; the analogy and place-dependent extension do not appear as claims about Goodman in the consulted primary passage.
claim_evidence.finding: The article labels these as an analogy and an extension rather than as Goodman’s own historical variants.
claim_evidence.limitation: These are editorial illustrations and are not independently evaluated here as technical AI claims.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: explicitly labelled both as teaching analogies/extensions.

edits_made: Made the future cutoff and examination condition in the grue definition explicit.
Separated Goodman’s projectibility problem from the broader justification problem for induction and identified the simplifying confirmation assumption.
Narrowed the entrenchment account and labeled the machine-learning and place-dependent constructions as editorial extensions.
Limited the naturalness discussion to Scholz’s specific proposal and labeled the Bayesian priors/model-class takeaway as an editorial inference.
Aligned the article’s five Further Reading URLs with the dataset record and matched the verification date.
unresolved: Whether any response fully resolves Goodman’s new riddle remains an active philosophical issue; the article summarizes a limited selection rather than a comprehensive survey.
The publisher endpoint for Fitelson’s final article was not extractable; the manuscript text and indexed bibliographic metadata were consulted instead.
The place-dependent and machine-learning examples are teaching extensions, not claims established by the cited sources.
entries.dataset_alignment: The grue data record’s five Further Reading URLs match the article’s five URLs in the same order, and date_verified matches the article research-check date 2026-11-01. No public source-review status field was added.
entries.further_reading_matches: All five article Further Reading URLs match the dataset record in the same order.
entries.risk_reason: The entry combines a technical definition, competing confirmation predictions, a subtle distinction between descriptive and normative accounts, and modern Bayesian/naturalness responses; the main risks were oversimplifying the cutoff or overstating a single contemporary proposal as a consensus solution.
entries.audit_focus: Check Goodman’s primary definition and entrenchment passages, distinguish Goodman’s problem from Hume’s broader question, verify each modern response against its source, and label unsourced extensions as editorial framing.
entries.independent_review: Final independent read-only review recommended source_checked for the declared material-claim scope. It confirmed the definition, entrenchment, positionality, specific naturalness critique, Bayesian qualifications, article/data URL order, and dates. The review found no material correction outstanding. No expert review.
